question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{3\pi }{2}]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{t}^{4}\cdot (2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4\,dt\end{aligned}
$$
